planting.note: Plant after last frost in rich, well-drained soil in full sun to partial shade, or grow as a houseplant in bright light; Gold Star croton needs strong light to hold its bright yellow leaf speckling.

directions: Plant after last frost in rich, well-drained soil in full sun to partial shade, or grow as a houseplant in bright light; Gold Star croton needs strong light to hold its bright yellow leaf speckling. Narrow, elongated, glossy green leaves are heavily speckled with bright golden-yellow spots that can nearly cover the leaf surface in strong light, one of the most vividly gold-toned of the many croton leaf-color selections and a striking accent among the deeper reds and oranges of other croton cultivars. Like other crotons it colors most intensely with abundant direct or bright indirect light, fading to duller green in low light, and it holds its foliage year-round in frost-free gardens or as a long-lived container and houseplant elsewhere. Water when the top inch of soil dries, protect from any frost, and wipe dust from the glossy leaves periodically to keep them looking their best.
sources: American Society for Horticultural Science reference

planting.note: Plant after last frost in rich, well-drained soil in full sun to partial shade, or grow as a houseplant in bright light; Oakleaf croton needs strong light to develop its best red and orange coloring.

directions: Plant after last frost in rich, well-drained soil in full sun to partial shade, or grow as a houseplant in bright light; Oakleaf croton needs strong light to develop its best red and orange coloring. Deeply lobed leaves with irregular, wavy margins closely resemble an oak leaf in outline, a distinctive leaf shape among crotons that are otherwise typically grown for solid or strap-shaped foliage, colored in a mix of green, gold, orange, and red that intensifies with age and bright light. Its unusual leaf shape adds textural variety to a mixed tropical planting or croton collection where most other selections offer only color variation on similar strap- or oval-shaped leaves. Water when the top inch of soil dries, provide bright light for the fullest color development, and protect from any frost.
sources: American Society for Horticultural Science reference

planting.note: Plant after last frost in rich, well-drained soil in partial shade to full sun, or grow as a houseplant in bright indirect light; Kiwi cordyline holds its variegation best out of the hottest afternoon sun.

directions: Plant after last frost in rich, well-drained soil in partial shade to full sun, or grow as a houseplant in bright indirect light; Kiwi cordyline holds its variegation best out of the hottest afternoon sun. Long, strap-shaped leaves are edged in cream and pink over a green center with a distinct thin magenta margin at the very edge, a layered, multi-toned variegation pattern reminiscent of the fruit for which it is named, borne on an upright, cane-like stem typical of ti plants. Native to the Pacific Islands and long culturally significant across Polynesia, ti plant is a classic tropical landscape and container shrub in frost-free climates, valued for its bold, colorful, low-maintenance foliage that needs no deadheading or special care beyond routine watering. Water when the top inch of soil dries, protect from any frost, and cut back leggy canes to encourage bushier new growth from the base.
sources: American Society for Horticultural Science reference

common_name: Red Star Cordyline (New Zealand Cabbage Palm)

planting.note: Plant container-grown stock in spring in well-drained soil in full sun; Red Star cordyline tolerates more cold and drought than tropical ti plant but is still frost-tender and best grown in a large container in cold climates.

directions: Plant container-grown stock in spring in well-drained soil in full sun; Red Star cordyline tolerates more cold and drought than tropical ti plant but is still frost-tender and best grown in a large container in cold climates. Narrow, sword-like, deep burgundy-red leaves radiate outward in a bold, spiky rosette atop a thickening trunk that develops a palm-like silhouette as the plant matures, giving strong architectural presence to a xeriscape or Mediterranean-style planting. More cold- and drought-tolerant than the tropical ti plant, it is native to New Zealand grassland and coastal habitats and handles brief light frost and dry spells better once established, though it is still killed by hard freezes outside its hardiness range. Water regularly while young and during extended drought, and grow in a large container to move under cover for winter outside zones 9-11.

planting.note: Plant after last frost in rich, well-drained soil in full sun to partial shade, or grow as a houseplant in bright indirect light; Renegade cordyline holds its deep burgundy color best with abundant light.

directions: Plant after last frost in rich, well-drained soil in full sun to partial shade, or grow as a houseplant in bright indirect light; Renegade cordyline holds its deep burgundy color best with abundant light. Narrow, glossy leaves emerge nearly solid deep burgundy-red to near-black, one of the darkest and most saturated color selections among cordyline cultivars, forming an upright, cane-like clump that provides bold, season-long color contrast against green-leaved companions in a tropical or container planting. Its compact size and reliably intense dark coloring, holding well through the season without fading to green in reasonable light, make it a popular choice for adding a strong color anchor to mixed tropical containers and landscape beds in frost-free climates. Water when the top inch of soil dries, provide bright light for the deepest color, and protect from any frost.
sources: American Society for Horticultural Science reference

planting.note: Grow as a houseplant or shaded patio container in bright, indirect light in well-drained potting mix; variegated screw pine develops sharp, tooth-edged leaves, so site it away from high-traffic areas and handle with care.

directions: Grow as a houseplant or shaded patio container in bright, indirect light in well-drained potting mix; variegated screw pine develops sharp, tooth-edged leaves, so site it away from high-traffic areas and handle with care. Long, arching, sword-shaped leaves striped in white and green spiral around a central growing point in a distinctive corkscrew pattern that gives the whole plant genus its common name, with fine, sharp spines along the leaf margins and midrib. As the plant matures it develops thick, stilt-like prop roots at the base that help anchor and support the increasingly top-heavy rosette, an unusual and architectural feature that adds to its appeal as a bold specimen plant for a bright room or shaded tropical patio. Wipe dust from the leaves carefully with gloves due to the sharp edges, water when the top inch of potting mix dries, and provide bright indirect light to maintain crisp variegation.
sources: American Society for Horticultural Science reference
